title: 'Why was he in a maximum-security prison?' Advocates want answers on immigration detainee's death in custody
subtitle: More than seven years later, an inquest will start Monday into the death of Abdurahman Ibrahim Hassan, a man with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
article: The final hours of the life of Abdurahman Ibrahim Hassan unfolded as a grim series of events - a human car crash, playing out in slow motion.

The Toronto man with a history of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder had been detained in Central East Correctional Centre, a maximum-security jail in Lindsay, Ont., for years awaiting deportation to Somalia when he was hospitalized in June 2015 "for medical reasons."
While held in the "isolation room" at the Peterborough Regional Health Centre, he smeared feces on the bed, his face, his forehead and his arms. He even ingested clumps of his own hair.

Two paid-duty officers - one from Peterborough Police Service, the other from the Ontario Provincial Police - entered the room with five nurses and three security guards to restrain and sedate him. He fell asleep in five minutes.
A couple of hours later, the same officers and four nurses returned to clean up the room. The 39-year-old awoke and a struggle ensued.

"While being restrained, the man kicked, hit, and grabbed at the nurses who were attempting to clean him and his bedding," said an investigation into the death of Hassan by the Special Investigations Unit, Ontario's police watchdog.
"Suddenly, the man stopped moving. It was determined that he was without vital signs and resuscitation efforts were performed."
A post-mortem examination was inconclusive as to the cause of his death.
More than seven years after Hassan died, a 15-day inquest will begin Monday to examine the events surrounding his death.

Although the SIU has cleared both officers of wrongdoing, advocates say there are many unanswered questions and hope the inquest could expose the plight of migrants with mental health needs caught up in an immigration detention system that some feel lacks transparency and accountability.

"All the questions remain unanswered starting from the very beginning: Why did he not receive the support and care he needed from the start when he came (here)? Why did he not get his citizenship and instead lose his refugee status?" asks Syed Hussan of the Migrant Rights Network.

"Why was he in a maximum-security prison in Ontario when he was arrested for federal immigration detention? Why was he not in a hospital in the first place? Why was he not provided care in the days leading up to his death?"

Hassan's family said he came on his own as a teen to Canada for refuge from Somalia in 1993. He was granted asylum in the mid-1990s but never became a permanent resident. His family later joined him in Canada and tried to keep him at home and out of trouble.

Hassan had been convicted of violent criminal offences starting in 1999 and was issued a deportation order in 2005. Following an assault conviction in 2012, he served another jail sentence before he was transferred into a provincial jail in Lindsay. He had been held there since, on the grounds he posed a danger to the public, and would unlikely appear for removal from Canada.
Hassan's family is not expected to participate in the inquest, but two advocacy groups - the Canadian Council for Refugees and Refugee Law Office - have been granted intervener status.

Although inquest recommendations are not legally binding, Janet Dench of the refugee council said the occasion is a rare chance for the public to examine the systemic issues within the Canada Border Services Agency, which is responsible for immigration enforcement and detention.
"CBSA continues to be one of the few forces in Canada that has the power of arrest and detention, and yet there's no independent oversight at all," Dench said.
"This is generally the best we can get, a recommendation and then to follow up on it, to try to bring it into effect."

The biggest issues that advocates hope Hassan's inquest will shed light on are the treatment of immigration detainees with mental health issues as well as the gaps in the shared responsibilities between the federal agency responsible for immigration enforcement and the provincial correctional services in charge of the detention.

"We want to encourage the coroner to look at it in the context of how people do fall between the cracks where neither the provincial government nor the federal government is really taking responsibility for people in situations of crisis," said Dench.

Over the past decade, there have been at least three inquests into the immigration detainee deaths in Canada, including that of Lucia Vega Jimenez, 42, a Mexican woman who took her own life in 2013 while being held in B.C. pending deportation; and of Francisco Romero Astorga, 39, a Chilean suffering from depression and substance abuse who died of an overdose in 2016 in a Milton, Ont., jail.

The Jimenez inquest jury, Dench said, made some important recommendations that called for detainees' improved access to legal counsel, medical services, support organizations and family visits as well as monitored access to phones and internet - things for which advocates have been fighting for years.

Esteban Romero Astorga said it was hard to get any information from Canadian border officials after his brother's death and the inquest helped address many of the family's questions. What's most important about the process, he said, was the systemic changes the jury recommended to avoid future deaths.
His brother was alone and undocumented in Canada when he was arrested by Peel police after he was caught stealing food at a Walmart, and later handed over to the border agency.
Astorga said it was painful to sit through the five-day hearings in 2017 and learn the details of his brother's final moments, which he has not shared with their elderly parents.

"Every single detail made me understand his life in detention, but it didn't have to be so hard," Astorga told the Star from Dubai, where he works. "Little things could have saved his life. Giving people mental health help and letting them make international calls to families could've made a difference.
"Those details are still haunting me."
Although government authorities are not obligated to implement inquest recommendations, Astorga said officials have the moral obligation and responsibility to the families to do so.
"What I would like to see ... is a statement from the high authorities who oversee the whole system, saying that we've made a mistake and we are working to change things," said Astorga.
"I would like to see that commitment more than just the recommendations."

The CBSA said it is committed to exercising its responsibility for detentions to the highest possible standards, with the physical and mental health and well-being of detainees, as well as the safety and security of Canadians, the main considerations.
In fact, the agency said 14 of the 17 jury recommendations from the Jimenez inquest directed at the CBSA have been fully addressed.

The agency is unable to have a mental health-care professional present when a detainee is informed of a removal date or to conduct another mental health assessment just before the person's deportation. Another recommendation restricting the scheduling of a detainee's pre-removal risk assessment also involves factors beyond CBSA's control.

(The six recommendations from the Astorga inquest only involved the Ontario Ministry of Community Safety and Correctional Services, which has adopted those suggestions, including intelligence gathering and searching for drugs and contrabands, improving telephone access and replacing segregation doors with redesigned meal hatch to make it harder to tamper with. However, the ministry was reviewing the introduction of calling cards and "door sweeps" to fill the gap under cell doors, hence unable to say at what phase they are at in terms of implementation.)

"The CBSA treats any death in custody very seriously. In line with internal policies, the CBSA reviews each incident, co-operates with any external investigation or inquests, and implements related recommendations when and where operationally feasible," the border agency said in a statement to the Star.

It said it has implemented the National Immigration Detention Framework to improve the detention system by opening a new holding centre in Surrey, B.C., and improving the detention facility in Toronto last year to ensure it complies with the new national immigration detention standards . It was also opening a new facility in Laval, Que.

Instead of relying on provincial jails to accommodate overflow of immigration detainees, these CBSA holding centres are all staffed by CBSA employees and contracted guards to ensure detention standards - such as access to legal counsel, medical services, community and spiritual support, and family visits - are followed.

Not only do detainees have free access to telephones and may request a calling card from staff to make long-distance calls, the agency said they are also provided with information in 16 languages about their rights and the detention review process, as well as contact information for legal aid, counsel and support groups. Policy is currently being developed and options explored on internet access for detainees.
Dedicated detention liaison officers meet detainees to regularly assess their well-being and answer questions with regard to their individual case.
"These changes demonstrate the ongoing commitment of CBSA to a more humane and fair immigration system without sacrificing public safety," the border agency said.

However, Hussan of the Migrant Rights Network said what Ottawa really needs to do is reflect on the whole premise of immigration detention, where people are jailed for administrative reasons pending removal from the country rather than for committing criminal offences.

"Abdurahman was there until CBSA could somehow deport him. He was detained indefinitely. And there was no way for him to get what he needed for his mental health problems. He was being imprisoned for no reason," said Hussan.

"Detention worsens people's mental health. If the federal government chooses to continue to jail migrants without trial or charges indefinitely and can't even keep them alive in its care, it needs to just step away from immigration detention."
